claims.text: Selective chemical dealloying of an NM-HEA precursor containing more-reactive sacrificial elements produces a three-dimensional nanoframework.
The resulting nanoframework has high surface area.
Dealloying provides controlled noble-metal distribution in the nanoframework.
The high surface area and controlled noble-metal distribution are beneficial for catalytic applications.
The precursor is a homogeneous bulk high-entropy alloy containing noble metals and less-noble sacrificial elements.
An acidic aqueous treatment can selectively dealloy the precursor.
Appropriately controlled acid concentration, temperature, and duration can dissolve sacrificial elements without collapsing the residual alloy structure.
Selective removal of sacrificial elements creates interconnected nanoscale porosity.
Acidic dealloying preferentially dissolves the more-reactive sacrificial elements.
Preferential dissolution leaves behind an interconnected porous noble-metal framework.
The dealloyed framework retains atomic-scale mixing.
The porous framework provides high exposure of catalytic surface sites.
Compared with untreated bulk NM-HEA, the dealloyed material has greater surface area and more accessible catalytic sites.
Effective nanoframework formation requires a sufficient precursor fraction of sacrificial elements.
Dealloying conditions must be tuned to avoid framework collapse or sintering.
The effects of dealloying parameters on uniform porosity and catalytic performance remain insufficiently quantified.
